newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka to offer major stake in Telecom monopoly.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka to offer major stake in Telecom monopoly.

text.p: Sri Lanka said on Thursday it will sell a major stake in a state telecommunications monopoly as part of the country's ambitious privatisation programme.

"Advertisements are going out locally and internationally within a week, calling for a strategic partner to take up a 35 percent stake and management in Sri Lanka Telecom," said Rajan Asirwatham, Chairman of the Public Enterprise Reform Commission.
Sri Lanka Telecom would be the most complex and largest privatisation the nation has embarked on, stock analysts said.
Asirwatham, who is in charge of government privatisation plans, indirectly ruled out any sale to a local investor by saying the offer would be limited to "experienced telecommunications operators".

He told Reuters that reforming Telecom topped the list of needy reforms in Sri Lanka's creaking infrastructure and was absolutely essential for a country canvassing foreign investment to generate jobs.
"Without reforming Telecom, Sri Lanka will go into the 21st century as one of the very few countries which cannot provide telephones even on payment," he said.
Sri Lanka's privatisation programme was set up under the Public Enterprise Reform Commission on March 1, 1995.

High points so far, include Royal Dutch Shell groups purchase of a controlling stake in Colombo Gas Co and Alpha Airports Group plc's purchase of a stake in airport duty-free operator Orient Lanka in early 1996.
The privatisation of 23 plantation firms started in late 1995, while Airlanka, the ailing national carrier, was restructured by a Chase Manhattan-led consortium.
Sri Lanka now has 226,200 direct telephone lines for a population of 18 million people, with a waiting list for about another 300,000 lines, analysts say.
Asirwatham said the sale of the 35 percent stake would be completed by the end of this year.
Restructuring Sri Lanka Telecom matches up with the government's stated goal of reforming non-profitable and badly managed public enterprises.
"Where a total or partial sell-off is not feasible, the government will try to end most monopolies by encouraging competition and reform others by injecting efficient management," Asirwatham said.
The sale of the Telecom stake was recommended by a consortium led by Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, commissioned by the government in April to restructure the state firm.

Other consortium members were Sri Lankan co-ordinators Development Finance Corporation, technical consultants Deloitte Touche Tomatsu International, and international legal consultants Slaughter and May.
Analysts speculated that a 35 percent stake and management of Sri Lanka Telecom could enrich state coffers by about 15 billion rupees ($268 million).
Sri Lanka Telecom's post-tax-profit in 1995 was 1.82 billion rupees and it employed 7,750 at the end of March this year.
Asirwatham also brushed aside fears that the unionised labour force would oppose reforms.
